events.description: Patents issued to Fred Ashley, Harris Low Cloud, Edward Face Darkling, Bull Tail, Thomas Larvie, Edward Quick Bear, Reuben Quick Bear, Joseph Runs Close to Village, and John Runs Close to Village. They disposed of land immediately and spent money within 6 months.
Multiple patents-in-fee issued to Fort Peck allottees, majority resulted in land loss and destitution.
Subsequent issuance of patents-in-fee largely to mixed blood element, practically all land disposed of.
Approximately 600 patents-in-fee issued beginning with mixed bloods and educated Indians.
Approximately 800 patents-in-fee issued to Rosebud Indians, estimated 10% made success.
Board of Indian Commissioners issued circular letter requesting information on patent-in-fee Indian conditions from Indian Service farmers.
Response letter to Board of Indian Commissioners regarding patent-in-fee conditions, writer on special detail purchasing cattle in Southwest.
First Enabling Act of 1905 led to allotments to heads of families on Standing Rock Reservation.
Children allotted lands under amendatory act, often 50-70 miles from parents' homes.
Children born after 1917 were not allotted 160 acres of land.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patent-in-fee issuance too liberal for Indians. Conditions far better before citizenship was given. Indians selling allotments outright or mortgaging for cash and automobiles. Recommended more careful examination and retaining homesteads.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Wolf Point Sub-agency, Fort Peck Indian Reservation
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions at Wolf Point
testimony.key_claims: Every Indian in district who received patent-in-fee has failed. No lands, no money, no homes. Some living with relatives for support, using children's money. Charles Owens sold 390 acres for $750 cash and livestock. Cleveland Owens sold 380 acres for horses and money. Ned and Lizzie Cantrell sold 740 acres and squandered money. Trust patent Indians like Henry Blacktail and Joshua Wets It have 40-80 head cattle and good homes. Recommended retaining at least 40 acres per individual.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions in Blackpipe District
testimony.key_claims: 33 patents issued in 8.5 years. Some Larvie family members retained land. Full-bloods not successful with patents. Quarter breeds who retained land did better. 1913 patentees disposed of land immediately and spent money within 6 months. Recommended retaining 100 acres minimum and strenuous examination.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions in Little White River District
testimony.key_claims: Almost all patent-in-fee Indians squandered land except four. First thing most do is get drunk and trade land for car and money. Those who sold bought automobiles used for joy-rides. Patent Indians come back to superintendent requesting patents on other allotments.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Rosebud Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Great mistake to let Indians sell all land. Should be allowed to dispose of inherited lands but compelled to hold own allotment for another 35 years. Majority sell lands as fast as they get patent. Some mortgage land for old automobiles, lose land when unable to pay. Indian experience with money handling may do them good in time but they are very slow to learn.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, 800 patents issued, 10% success
testimony.key_claims: About 800 patents-in-fee issued on Rosebud. Not more than 10% made success. Large majority would have been far better off if land retained in trust. Of 21 patent-in-fee Indians in his district, only 3 did not sell. Fourteen of twenty-one sold lands and spent money. One sold for $6,200 and reinvested. One sold for $4,000 and partly reinvested. Recommended allowing sale of inherited lands through Office with supervision, retaining white settlement as good example.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, benefits of independence
testimony.key_claims: Indian will make no material progress until placed on own resources. Too much dependence on Government guardianship. After patent, Indians have nothing to sit and wait for. 90% squander land but then settle down. Knows dozens who squandered at least part but settled down and joined white community. Nearly all Indians more than half white made success. Cited full-blood typist employee who improved after receiving patent. 59 names submitted of benefited Indians. Recommended issuing fee patents for own land since children's lands still available.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer or official, Rosebud Indian Agency
testimony.subject: Individual examination and trust retention policy
testimony.key_claims: Strongly favors individual examination for each patent applicant. Many Indians realize they would be better off if property still held in trust. Recommends at least 40 acres retained in trust with clause compelling building of house and barn. Without restriction, Indians sell land or mortgage for one-third value, buy automobile, lose land when loan due. William Simpson and wife have no home, land sold. William Bordeaux and wife have no home, living hand to mouth. Todd Smith sold $13,000 of land, has only $300 house.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, learning through experience
testimony.key_claims: Believes more probability of Indians succeeding if they must depend on themselves. Cited full-blood young man who sold patent, bought car and stock, exhausted funds, returned to work and became best employee. Another full-blood sold two fee patents, using proceeds to improve wife's quarter. Indians sow wild oats then settle down.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, four years experience
testimony.key_claims: Grave question with as much against as for it. In four years knows few who did not sell and blow money. Small number making homes on land. Individual examination recommended. Should not turn all loose as most would be in poor house or begging, burden to state or county. Real estate men pester Indians until they sell.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Standing Rock Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 patents-in-fee issued on Standing Rock. First issuance to mixed bloods and educated Indians before 1915 resulted in most immediately disposing of land. 1916 issuance largely to mixed blood element, practically all disposed of. Indians permitted themselves to be involved in mortgages. Only one Indian (Nation Flying) known to have made good. Many Indians received allotments 50-70 miles from parents' home, making land useless. Children allotted in 1908-1909 had no knowledge of their allotments. Many sold for no other reason than land was useless to them. White people felt administration period was one of private gain.

mortgages.context: General pattern described: Indians mortgage land for one-third of value, buy automobile, unable to meet obligation when due, lender gets land at considerably less than actual value. Described by Rosebud Agency farmer.

mortgages.land_description: patented allotment lands on Fort Peck Reservation

mortgages.land_description: patented lands on Standing Rock Reservation
mortgages.context: Standing Rock patentees permitted themselves to be involved in mortgages, interest and principal gradually ate up resources, necessary to dispose of land entirely. Only one Indian known to have regained allotment after mortgage.
